opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's been a long and winding road. When we started OpenCog Classic, way back, the idea was fairly straightforward conceptually: you have a knowledge hypergraph, the Atomspace, and multiple cognitive algorithms acting on it together. Probabilistic logic, evolutionary program learning, attention allocation, pattern mining. The theory was that the synergy between these processes, each helping the others out of their combinatorial dead ends, is what gives you general intelligence.

What we learned is that the theory held up reasonably well, but the infrastructure didn't. The original Atomspace wasn't fast enough or distributed enough, and the way we glued the algorithms together was ad hoc. Each component had its own representations and quirks, so "cognitive synergy" was more aspiration than implementation.

So Hyperon was really a rethink from the ground up. The key move was MeTTa, a language whose programs are themselves stored in the Atomspace and can be reasoned about, rewritten and learned by the system itself. That's critical, because I think a real AGI has to be able to reflect on and modify its own cognitive processes, not just its data. You want the logic engine, the program learner and the pattern miner all expressed in a common substrate so they can actually interoperate at a fine-grained level.

The other big lesson is scale. You can have elegant cognitive architecture, but if it runs on one machine at hobbyist speed, you'll never find out whether it works. That's why we've put so much effort into distributed Atomspace backends, specialized hardware collaborations, and running this on decentralized infrastructure like SingularityNET, rather than depending on a single big tech data center.

And of course the LLM revolution changed the picture too. I don't think transformers alone get you to AGI. They're amazing at pattern completion, but weak at grounded reasoning, novel abstraction and stable self-modeling. Still, they're tremendously useful components. So the stack I now envision is hybrid: neural models for perception, language and broad associative knowledge, plugged into a symbolic-probabilistic metagraph core that does the reasoning, goal management and self-reflection. Hyperon is designed to be that core.

So in short, building it has convinced me that the hard part isn't any single algorithm. It's the representational substrate and the plumbing that let many kinds of learning and reasoning work together, scalably and reflectively. Get that right, and I think the path to human-level AGI, and beyond, gets a lot shorter than people expect.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. It's a good question, because building Hyperon has actually changed my views quite a bit, not so much about what AGI is, but about what you actually need underneath it to make it work in practice.

The original OpenCog, going back to the 2008 timeframe, was built around what we called the AtomSpace, a weighted, labeled hypergraph knowledge store, with a bunch of different cognitive processes operating on it: probabilistic logic, evolutionary program learning, attention allocation, and so forth. And conceptually, that architecture held up fairly well. The problem was that the software substrate couldn't carry the weight of the ideas. Everything was written in a tangle of C++ and Scheme and Python, the AtomSpace didn't scale across machines, and every cognitive algorithm had its own idiosyncratic way of representing things. So you'd spend most of your time fighting the infrastructure rather than doing cognitive science.

Hyperon was a decision to rebuild from the foundations. The core realization was that if you want many different learning and reasoning algorithms to genuinely cooperate on a shared knowledge base, you need a common language they can all speak, down to the level of the atoms themselves. That's where MeTTa came from, Meta Type Talk. It's a language where the knowledge, the inference rules, and the programs that manipulate the knowledge are all just atoms in the same space, and type systems can be dependently typed, or probabilistic, or whatever the task calls for. Once you have that, a logic engine and a neural network and an evolutionary learner can actually read and write each other's intermediate results, instead of passing messages across some brittle API.

The second thing building it taught me is that the scaling story is non-negotiable. Pure symbolic systems failed in the past partly because they were small. So a big part of the Hyperon effort has been the distributed AtomSpace, and thinking about dedicated hardware for pattern matching and graph rewriting, because the operations a cognitive synergy architecture does constantly are quite different from the dense matrix multiplies that GPUs are optimized for.

And the third thing, frankly, is that large language models arriving in the middle of this process clarified the stack rather than undermining it. LLMs are extraordinary at certain things and quite poor at others, like reliable multi-step reasoning or knowing what they don't know. In Hyperon they become one component among several, feeding into the AtomSpace, getting their outputs checked and refined by probabilistic logic, and in turn being guided by symbolic representations. So the stack ends up being a layered one: a shared knowledge representation at the bottom, a metalanguage to express everything, a scalable distributed store, and then a diverse ecology of cognitive processes on top. I think that's roughly what you need, and I don't think any one of those layers alone gets you to AGI.

astra-6.text:
Building OpenCog Hyperon has reinforced my view that AGI is an architecture problem as much as it is a learning-algorithm problem. You need learning, reasoning, memory, perception, and action, but having each of those components individually is not enough. They need to help each other solve problems.

A neural system might recognize a pattern that a reasoning system can turn into a hypothesis. Reasoning might identify something the system doesn’t understand, which then guides what it learns or explores next. I call that cognitive synergy. The interesting question is how to make that interaction productive rather than just connecting a bunch of modules and hoping intelligence emerges.

And that takes you surprisingly far down the technology stack. How do you represent knowledge so different processes can work on it? How do you make those processes run efficiently? How do you preserve flexibility without making every operation prohibitively expensive? Those infrastructure choices shape which cognitive experiments you can actually do.

So I’ve become more convinced that you have to develop the cognitive architecture and the underlying software together. You need an idea of how intelligence works, but you also need to keep revising that idea through building systems and seeing where they fail.

sol-6.1.text:
Building OpenCog Hyperon has reinforced my view that AGI isn’t just about finding one magical learning algorithm. You need a system in which different kinds of intelligence can work together: learning from experience, reasoning, forming abstractions, and deciding what to do.

The challenge is that putting those capabilities in separate boxes and connecting them with APIs doesn’t necessarily give you an integrated mind. They need to share representations and help one another overcome their limitations. A reasoning process might get stuck, and pattern recognition can suggest a direction; learning might need reasoning to make sense of a situation it hasn’t encountered before. That’s the kind of interaction I mean by cognitive synergy.

So the technology stack has to support that interaction all the way down. You need flexible knowledge representation, efficient execution, and ways to integrate neural learning with symbolic reasoning without forcing everything into one rigid paradigm. And you need to experiment with the whole system, because a collection of individually impressive components doesn’t automatically become generally intelligent. The architecture matters, but so does how those components develop together through experience.
